ready1_open_rewrite.title: SciVerse open question
ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: A student designed an experiment intended to determine the specific heat capacity of aluminum. During the experiment, an aluminum block with a mass of $5.86\ \mathrm{g}$ was heated to different temperatures, and then it was immersed in a calorimeter containing $25.0\ \mathrm{mL}$ of water. The table below shows the data collected during one of the trials. It is known that the specific heat capacity of aluminum is $0.900\ \mathrm{J/(g\cdot^\circ C)}$; please calculate the percent error of this trial. (The final answer is a numerical value)

Reasoning: The problem stem gives the mass of the aluminum block m_Al=5.86 g, and the volume of water is 25.0 mL; using the water density 1.00 g/mL gives water mass m_water=25.0 g; the true specific heat capacity of aluminum is 0.900 J/(g·°C). The temperature increase of water ΔT_water=26.8-23.2=3.6 °C; the temperature decrease of aluminum ΔT_Al=109.1-26.8=82.3 °C. The heat absorbed by water q_water=m_water c_water ΔT_water=25.0×4.18×3.6=376.2 J. Let the heat absorbed by water be equal to the heat released by aluminum: q_water=m_Al c_Al,exp ΔT_Al, so c_Al,exp=376.2/(5.86×82.3)≈0.780 J/(g·°C). Percent error=|0.780-0.900|/0.900×100%≈13.3%.
